topic.subject: science
topic.title: Physical and chemical changes
topic.scope: reversible and irreversible changes, signs of chemical change, rusting, crystallisation, burning

misconceptions.statement: All changes that look different are irreversible.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse the visual appearance of an object with the permanence of the change.
misconceptions.fix: A change is reversible if the original substance can be recovered through simple physical methods, regardless of how different it looks.

probe.question: If you fold a piece of paper into a boat, can you get the paper back?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the paper has changed its shape and is now a boat.

misconceptions.statement: If a change happens quickly, it must be reversible.
misconceptions.why: Students associate speed with the ease of undoing an action in daily life.
misconceptions.fix: The speed of a change has no relation to whether it can be reversed; some fast changes like burning are permanent.

probe.question: Is lighting a matchstick a reversible change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it happens very quickly.

misconceptions.statement: A physical change always involves a change in the state of matter.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often use melting ice as the primary example of a physical change.
misconceptions.fix: Physical changes include any change in shape, size, or state where no new substance is formed.

probe.question: Is cutting a piece of wood into small sawdust a physical change?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the wood did not melt or freeze.

misconceptions.statement: If a new color appears, it is always a chemical change.
misconceptions.why: Students are taught that color change is a sign of a chemical reaction, leading them to ignore physical mixing.
misconceptions.fix: Color change is only a sign of a chemical change if it indicates the formation of a new substance, not just mixing two colored liquids.

probe.question: If I mix blue ink and yellow ink to get green ink, is it a chemical change?

misconceptions.statement: Burning is a physical change because the object just gets smaller.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the reduction in size rather than the production of ash and smoke.
misconceptions.fix: Burning is a chemical change because it produces entirely new substances like ash and gases that cannot be turned back into the original material.

probe.question: Why is burning a piece of paper a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not; it is just a physical change because the paper got smaller.

misconceptions.statement: Rust is just dirt that collects on iron.
misconceptions.why: Rust looks like brown dust or soil, and students observe it accumulating on surfaces.
misconceptions.fix: Rust is a new substance formed by the chemical reaction between iron, oxygen, and water.

probe.question: Can you wash rust off iron like you wash off mud?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, rust is just dirty particles stuck to the metal.

misconceptions.statement: Crystallisation is a chemical change because the crystals look different from the powder.
misconceptions.why: The dramatic change in appearance from a powder to a crystal suggests a chemical transformation to students.
misconceptions.fix: Crystallisation is a physical change because the substance remains the same chemically; only its physical form changes.

probe.question: Is obtaining salt crystals from a salt solution a chemical change?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the salt looks like a crystal now instead of a powder.
